New figures from the British Retail Consortium (BRC) and Sensormatic have shown that UK retail footfall continued to decline in July, with extreme heat impacting visits to high streets.
Total UK footfall fell 2.1 percent year-on-year during the four weeks to August 1, improving from the 3.4 percent decline recorded in June.
High streets saw the largest decline, with footfall down 3.8 percent compared with the same period last year. Shopping centre visits fell 1.4 percent, while retail parks were the only destination type to record growth, increasing 1.2 percent year-on-year.
Scotland and Northern Ireland recorded increases in footfall, up 2.7 percent and 2.6 percent respectively, while Wales remained flat. England saw footfall decline by 3 percent, with London down 5.3 percent.
In a statement, BRC chief executive Helen Dickinson said the heatwave had “continued to bear down on retail footfall”, particularly affecting high streets as consumers avoided travel during soaring temperatures.
Sensormatic’s Andy Sumpter said the hot and dry weather had likely contributed to fewer shopping trips, but noted that retail parks had returned to growth, suggesting consumers were still visiting retail destinations despite making fewer overall trips.

Temperatures will ease slightly from near 40 C, but much of western Korea will remain hot despite heavy rain hitting the east coast
South Korea’s near-40 degrees Celsius temperatures are expected to ease slightly over the weekend, but there will be no real break from the heat.
Western regions will remain sweltering, while heavy rain could bring more than 150 millimeters to parts of the east coast through Sunday.
Friday
Seoul heads toward 39 C
Seoul and Jeonju were forecast to reach 39 degrees Celsius on Friday, with Incheon and Gwangju hitting 38 C and Daejeon and Daegu 37 C.
Temperatures had already climbed to around 30 C in several major cities by 8 a.m. after another tropical night.
Friday, which marks Ipchu, traditionally considered the beginning of autumn, could become the hottest Ipchu ever recorded in Seoul. The previous record was 35.9 C in 2018.
Highest-level heat warnings remain in effect for Seoul, parts of Gyeonggi Province, inland Gangwon Province and some southwestern areas.
Saturday
Showers inland, rain in the east
Temperatures are expected to fall slightly Saturday as clouds block some of the intense sunlight, but daytime highs will still hover around 35 C in many areas.
Rain will begin before dawn along the east coast of Gangwon Province and in nearby mountain areas before spreading to parts of the North Gyeongsang coast and Jeju.
Scattered afternoon showers of 5 to 40 mm are also forecast across Seoul, Incheon, Gyeonggi Province and inland areas nationwide.
The rain may briefly lower temperatures, but higher humidity afterward could make conditions feel just as uncomfortable.
Sunday
Heavy rain along east coast
Rain will continue Sunday along the east coast, in parts of the southeast and on Jeju Island.
The Gangwon coast and mountain areas are forecast to receive 30-100 mm from Saturday through Sunday, with more than 150 mm possible in some locations.
Northern coastal areas of North Gyeongsang Province could receive 30-80 mm, while 20-60 mm is expected farther south.
Flooding, landslides and swollen streams are possible in those areas.
Western Korea, however, will remain hot. Easterly winds crossing the Taebaek Mountains are expected to become warmer and drier, keeping apparent temperatures near 35 C.
What to know before heading out
Tropical nights are expected to continue through the weekend, meaning overnight temperatures staying above 25 C in many areas.
People planning outdoor activities Saturday should prepare for sudden showers, while travelers heading to Gangwon Province or the east coast should check rainfall and road conditions.
Strong winds, high waves and swells are also expected around Jeju and parts of the southern and eastern coasts. Beachgoers should avoid rocks, breakwaters and exposed coastal roads.

Heatwave hampers high street footfall in July as consumers ‘stay home’
The ongoing heatwave has put another thorn in the side of UK retailers, with high street footfall particularly affected, down 3.8% year-on-year in July, though that was up from -6.2% in June, when the extreme warm weather first hit.
That’s according to the latest data from the BRC-Sensormatic Footfall Monitor, covering the four weeks from 5 July to 1 August, which revealed that total UK footfall decreased by 2.1% year-on-year in July (up from -3.4% in June).
Footfall in shopping centres also declined by 1.4% year-on-year in July, while retail parks saw a drop of 1.2%.
Helen Dickinson, Chief Executive of the British Retail Consortium, said: "The heatwave continued to bear down on retail footfall in July, with high streets worst affected. London was hit particularly hard as soaring temperatures made tube and train travel less attractive, with some commuters and shoppers opting to stay home.
"Nonetheless, it was still an improvement on the previous month’s figures, when record-breaking sunshine saw footfall fall by an even bigger margin.
"Climate change continues to deliver more and more extreme temperatures in the UK. Retailers are responding by investing in both mitigations – such as more air conditioning and more efficient refrigeration units – and in sustainability initiatives aimed at reducing carbon emissions.
"Unfortunately, business rates often punish stores for such investments, showing the need for government to look again at this broken system.”
Andy Sumpter, Head of Consulting & Analytics - EMEA for Sensormatic, added: “July saw UK retail footfall remain under pressure, with total visits down 2.1% year-on-year. While this represents an improvement on June’s -3.4%, the broader trend remains challenging, with six of the first seven months of 2026 performing worse than the same period last year.
“The exceptionally hot and historically dry weather is likely to have been a significant factor, discouraging shopping trips and particularly impacting high streets.
“England recorded the weakest performance of any UK nation at -3%, with London down 5.3%, highlighting the continued challenges facing larger urban centres during periods of extreme heat.
“While the UK has yet another new Prime Minister, retail is yet to experience any meaningful 'Burnham Bounce'. For retailers, the focus remains on converting these more selective visits into meaningful spend as the summer progresses.”

Lee ordered ministries and local governments to mobilise all available personnel and resources until the heatwave eases, stressing protection of lives and safety, stronger safeguards for vulnerable residents and stricter enforcement of rest breaks for outdoor workers during the hottest hours.
The warning came as Seoul endured another stifling night before what forecasters say could be one of the hottest days in the city's modern history.

Meteorologists say Typhoon Dolphin, despite posing no direct threat to South Korea, may be contributing to the scorching conditions.

The drones hover over the farmers, broadcasting warnings such as "it's hot, you need to go inside" to remind them to take breaks and cool down.

Number of summer wildfires rises as temperatures do the same
A Korea Forest Service official explained that "a prolonged drought and extreme heat rapidly reduce moisture levels in trees and forests, which increases the risk of wildfires."
Firefighters work on a burning area near Loumpa as wildfires hit West Attica, Greece, on Aug. 3.REUTERS/YONHAP
Wildfires are breaking out across Korea as temperatures approach 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit), with the prolonged heat and drought leaving forests increasingly dry and vulnerable to fire.
A wildfire broke out in Gurye County, South Jeolla, at approximately 9:58 a.m. on Friday, according to the Korea Forest Service (KFS) and fire authorities — only a day after another broke out in Hamyang County, South Gyeongsang, and Muju County, North Jeolla, in the afternoon.
Both were extinguished within an hour and burned less than 1 hectare (2.5 acres) of land.
Earlier, a wildfire broke out on a mountain in Dalseong County, Daegu, at around 5:18 p.m. on Monday and was extinguished within approximately 30 minutes. That same day, a fire at a waste recycling facility in Yeongcheon, North Gyeongsang, spread to a nearby mountain before firefighters brought it under control about an hour later.
Three wildfires also broke out in Ulju County, Ulsan, between July 24 and Sunday.
A fire in a reed field near the Mangyeong River in Gimje, North Jeolla, on Saturday burned about 200 hectares before it was extinguished 17 hours later.
Summer wildfires have become increasingly common in recent years. The number of wildfires recorded between June and August rose from 12 in 2023 to 35 in 2024 and 46 in 2025, according to the KFS.
Korea has already recorded 31 summer wildfires this year as of Friday.
Experts blame the extreme heat and drought, which have reduced moisture levels in forests.
Daegu received 165.1 millimeters (6.5 inches) of rain during June and July — only about 40 percent of the 411.7 millimeters recorded during the same period last year. Similarly, South Gyeongsang received 162 millimeters of rain over the two months, just 33.5 percent of its usual 483 millimeters. Ulsan recorded only 28 millimeters of rainfall in July, about 12 percent of its average of 234.1 millimeters.
Rising temperatures are also increasing wildfire risks, as a 2-degree Celsius increase in average temperatures raises the likelihood of wildfires by 13.5 percent, according to the KFS.
“Korea’s forests hold an amount of water equivalent to 10 times the capacity of Soyang Dam [in Gangwon],” Nam Sung-hyun, a former minister of the KFS, explained. “But prolonged drought and extreme heat rapidly reduce moisture levels in trees and forests, which increases the risk of wildfires.”
Other countries have also seen an increase in summer wildfires as temperatures rise.
“Korea is no longer a haven from the large summer wildfires that have recently occurred in Europe and the United States,” Nam added.
In response, local governments are stepping up wildfire prevention efforts.
Daegu expanded its specialized wildfire response team in July to strengthen its emergency response capacity. South Gyeongsang urged cities and counties to establish comprehensive summer wildfire prevention plans.
Such preventive measures are unusual during the summer because prevention efforts typically focus on the period from autumn through the following spring.
With fewer dedicated wildfire personnel assigned during the summer, Ulsan has turned to its forest disaster response team. The team, which responds to both wildfires and landslides, will inspect firefighting vehicles and run training exercises throughout the summer.
Anyone responsible for starting a wildfire can face up to three years in prison or a fine of up to 30 million won ($21,100) under the Forest Protection Act, even if the fire was caused by negligence.
“During the summer, prolonged drought and high temperatures can dry out fallen leaves in forests, which could ignite a wildfire with a small spark,” a KFS official said. “We urge the public not to burn trash or smoke in or near forested areas.”

Korean professional baseball is taking a break through Sunday as extreme heat continues across the country.
The KBO called off all 15 KBO League games scheduled between Friday and Sunday at five stadiums. The general managers of all 10 clubs and the secretary general of the Korea Professional Baseball Players Association made the decision at an emergency meeting on Thursday at the sport's headquarters in Gangnam District, southern Seoul.
That brings the number of games lost to heat this season to 30. The KBO had already scrapped every game on Wednesday and Thursday over concerns for the safety of spectators and players. Counting rainouts and other causes, 55 games have now been called off.
The KBO and the clubs will spend the weekend working out detailed heat measures and installing equipment before the league resumes on Tuesday with adjusted start times. First pitch, currently 6:30 p.m. on weekdays and 6 p.m. on weekends, moves to 7 p.m. across the board for the time being. Gocheok Sky Dome in Seoul, the league's only indoor venue, is the exception: 7 p.m. on weekdays, 6 p.m. on Saturdays and, depending on broadcast arrangements, as early as 2 p.m. on Sundays.
The league also laid out when games can go ahead. A game is called off at once if a heat wave emergency warning, the top tier of the three-level alert system, is in force at the stadium's location before 1 p.m. on the day.
Under a heat wave advisory or warning, an operations officer measures the apparent temperature at the ground from 1 p.m. onward. If the "feels like" reading at first pitch reaches 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit), or the officer judges the risk to be high, the game can be called off up to three hours before the start or pushed back to as late as 7:30 p.m. Once a game is underway, the decision to suspend or continue rests on the "feels like" reading together with the condition of players and spectators.
Every stadium will also introduce a cooling break. The changeover after the third and seventh innings stretches to four minutes to guarantee rest, and the cleaning time after the fifth can run up to six minutes where needed. Games that go to extra innings get another four minutes after the ninth.
Measures for spectators were expanded as well. Gates will open on a flexible schedule to cut the time fans spend waiting outside, and clubs will add canopies, misting fans, drinking water points and extra emergency medical staff. A hotline between the KBO and club safety officers will track heat-related illness at the grounds in real time.
The KBO had issued a tiered set of operating rules on Tuesday, under which games would go ahead as normal during a heat wave advisory and, under a heat wave warning, first pitch could be pushed back by up to an hour at the home club's request. Under those rules, a heat wave emergency warning before 1 p.m. required cancellation. The first games called off under the new system were at Jamsil Baseball Stadium in Seoul and in Gwangju on Tuesday.

[Sportschosun, Reporter Jang Jong-ho] As the heat wave drags on day after day, the risk of heat-related illness and dehydration is rising.
In particular, people with chronic conditions such as high blood pressure and diabetes need to be extra careful, as heat can cause blood pressure and blood sugar levels to fluctuate far more than usual. Dehydration does not simply cause thirst; it can also increase the risk of dizziness, falls, and cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease.
Medical staff at Seoul National University Hospital emphasized that, to stay healthy during extreme heat, it is most important to drink enough water to prevent dehydration and not miss warning signs from the body.
◇For patients with high blood pressure in extreme heat, the biggest enemy is dehydration
For people with high blood pressure, the greatest concern during a heat wave is dehydration. When the body lacks water, blood pressure can drop and blood flow to the brain can decrease, leading to dizziness or reduced consciousness. In particular, standing up suddenly after sitting, or rising from a lying position, can trigger orthostatic hypotension and increase the risk of collapse. If that leads to a fall, it can become a serious accident.
It is easy to assume that heavy sweating means you should also replenish a lot of salt, but that is a common misconception. The salt concentration in sweat is lower than in blood, so the more you sweat, the more concentrated the salt in your blood becomes. For that reason, it is better to drink water frequently and sufficiently rather than consume more salt. You should also avoid frequently eating salty foods such as cold noodle broth when you feel thirsty. Broth-based foods are high in sodium and can actually raise blood pressure.
Professor Lee Hae-young, a cardiologist, said, "Even if blood pressure is measured lower than usual in summer, you should not reduce or stop your medication on your own." She added, "First, try replenishing fluids sufficiently. If blood pressure still remains low, it is safest to consult your doctor and discuss adjusting the medication."
◇For people with chronic diseases, lifestyle management comes before medication
Extreme heat affects not only blood pressure but also blood sugar. If diarrhea, alcohol consumption, or caffeine intake is added to a state in which blood volume has already decreased through sweating, the risk of dehydration rises further. As the blood becomes thicker, the risk of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease can also increase. For that reason, it is best to avoid prolonged outdoor activity or work in hot, enclosed spaces whenever possible.
In particular, people taking blood pressure medication may experience low blood pressure or dizziness if dehydration is added on top. If you feel dizzy when standing up, if your blood pressure is much lower than usual, or if you experience severe palpitations or fainting, you should not adjust the medication yourself. Instead, consult your doctor. Diuretics control blood pressure by increasing urine output, so they carry a risk of dehydration and electrolyte imbalance. Diabetes treatments in the SGLT2 inhibitor class can also cause fluid loss as they help excrete sugar through urine, so people should pay even closer attention to fluid intake in summer.
Regular meals are just as important as drinking enough water. Even if the heat makes you lose your appetite, skipping meals can reduce the body's ability to maintain fluid balance. For older adults in particular, missing meals can weaken the body and also impair digestion, often leading to loose stools, which can further raise the risk of dehydration. When digestion is poor, appropriate medication such as gastrointestinal motility agents may help.
Meals should generally focus on easy-to-digest proteins such as white fish or lean meat, while greasy foods and excessive drinking should be reduced. However, if fruit and vegetable intake becomes excessive, some people taking blood pressure medication may see their potassium levels rise, so caution is needed.
Along with dietary management, it is also important to adjust daily activity and indoor conditions. During periods of extreme heat, it is advisable to reduce aerobic exercise by 20 to 30 percent and get enough rest. Indoors, maintaining temperature and humidity with proper air conditioning is also important to reduce strain on the heart and blood vessels.
Professor Min-sun Park of the Department of Family Medicine (FM) said, "If your blood pressure drops in summer, you should not stop or reduce your blood pressure or diabetes medication on your own." She added, "The safest approach is to record both your blood pressure and symptoms, then consult your doctor and adjust treatment according to your individual condition."
◇It is dangerous to dismiss it as 'just the heat'... Seek immediate medical care if these symptoms appear
Most heat-related illnesses improve if you rest in a cool place and replenish fluids adequately. However, if not handled properly, they can progress to life-threatening heatstroke, so it is important not to miss the early warning signs.
In particular, if your body temperature rises above 40°C and you begin to stagger due to ataxia, or if unusual behavior or aggression appears, heatstroke should be suspected even if there is no loss of consciousness. In addition, if headaches, dizziness, nausea, or vomiting persist, or if severe muscle cramps, rapid pulse, or shortness of breath occur, you should seek medical attention without delay.
Another factor to watch is the sudden temperature change when moving from outdoors to indoors. Sharp temperature differences affect peripheral blood vessels and the autonomic nervous system, placing a heavy burden on the cardiovascular system. In particular, on days when the temperature exceeds 35°C, a fan alone is not enough to prevent heat-related illness for high-risk groups such as older adults. Rather than enduring the heat, it is better to use air conditioning actively and keep indoor temperatures within a safe range.
Professor Kim Tae-gyun of Emergency Medicine (EM) said, "If body temperature exceeds 40°C and unusual behavior or changes in consciousness appear, you should consider the possibility of heatstroke and seek immediate medical care." He added, "During heat waves, preventing dehydration through sufficient fluid intake and rest, and never dismissing warning signs from the body, is above all the most important thing."

Heatstroke may be contributing to hospital overcrowding in Ireland
Almost 9,500 people aged 75 or over waited longer than 24 hours to get a hospital bed this year, as climate change-induced heatstroke now becomes a factor that health chiefs must grapple with.
The HSE said seasonal factors can affect numbers, “including health complications of heat stress”, but that no single factor is driving the summer surge that has led to what advocates call “stark” and “hugely concerning” figures from hospital emergency departments so far this year.
It has warned of risks of “dehydration, heat exhaustion, and heatstroke” — especially for older people and other vulnerable people. Met Éireann said July was the second hottest since 1900.
The HSE said: “Factors driving emergency department attendances and waiting times are complex. Seasonal factors may influence attendances, including health complications of heat stress, but as a specific factor, this is difficult to disaggregate from data available.”
Read More
Overall, 27,791 patients spent more than 24 hours in an emergency department between January and June. In addition, 58,894 left without being seen, including 10,650 for May alone.
However, delays facing older patients have raised serious concerns.
In June at Cork University Hospital, some 231 over-75s spent longer than 24 hours in the emergency department. At University Hospital Kerry, it stood at 31.
In University Hospital Limerick, 59 older patients waited that long. University Hospital Waterford was one of only four hospitals without patients in this category in June. The highest was St Vincent’s University Hospital in Dublin, which saw 178.
Delays increase risk of mortality
Studies repeatedly show negative effects from these delays, including the risk of increased mortality and death.
Camille Loftus, head of advocacy and public affairs at Age Action, said: “It is a horrendous situation for anybody, but if you’re older and unwell, that’s an even more difficult situation to manage.
She said there is “clearly a need for more beds” and called for more support for preventative medicine programmes.
“We’d like to see that because it will help reduce admissions but it’s never going to eliminate them,” she said. “And 24 hours is an enormous length of time to wait.”
The data was released to Sinn Féin health spokesman David Cullinane, who said the figures are “very stark”.
He warned: “This is not just a winter crisis anymore. The figures for older people are especially worrying. Almost 9,500 patients aged 75 and over waited more than 24 hours.
Nearly 59,000 people leaving an emergency department without being seen “should be a major warning sign for the Government”, he said, adding: “People do not leave an emergency department for no reason. In many cases, they have been waiting too long and feel they have no other option.”
At Mercy University Hospital in Cork, between 203 and 318 people left early every month. Similarly, at Tipperary University Hospital, between 143 and 222 people left. At University Hospital Waterford, between 225 and 400 left monthly.
“The staff are doing their best in very difficult conditions,” Mr Cullinane said.
He called for Government funding for published plans for “thousands of new hospital beds”, saying “announcing beds is not the same as building and staffing them”.
A spokesperson for HSE Dublin and South-East said its hospitals saw just over 10,000 more patients this year so far.
She linked the pressures to more older patients, seasonal illness, and “higher numbers of acute injuries and illnesses”.
In contrast, at Children’s Health Ireland, summer activity is as expected, despite a 2.7% jump in numbers compared to last year.
Its patient time in emergency departments is “improving all the time”, and it has seen a significant decline in the number of children leaving early.
- Niamh Griffin, Health Correspondent

The advisory urged people living in areas prone to sea erosion or inundation to move to safer places if directed by authorities.
Small boats and country craft have been advised not to venture into the sea. Fishermen have also been cautioned against launching or bringing fishing vessels ashore when wave activity intensifies.
Kerala Revenue Minister A P Anil Kumar visited relief camps in Alappuzha and Pathanamthitta districts on Thursday and said the government would extend all possible assistance to people affected by the recent rains and floods.
The minister said house-cleaning assistance would be provided to all affected families irrespective of whether they stayed in relief camps, with relatives or elsewhere after floodwaters entered their homes.
He said traders whose shops were inundated would receive Rs 10,000 each to help them resume business.
The minister said the existing loan scheme for traders would be revised and financial assistance for crop loss enhanced by 25 per cent.
Anil Kumar said the Revenue Department, Local Self-Government Department and other agencies, along with elected representatives and voluntary organisations, had effectively coordinated relief and rescue operations.
He said damaged roads would be restored after an assessment of losses and the works included under the disaster relief fund.
The minister said rescue operations remained the immediate priority during a disaster, after which revenue officials would conduct a detailed assessment of the damage.
He added that elected representatives were playing a key role in identifying affected households and assessing the extent of losses.
The minister later inspected the Thottappally Spillway in Alappuzha and reviewed measures being taken to ensure the smooth discharge of floodwaters into the sea.

Kerala remained on high alert as relentless rains disrupted normal life across the state, with the IMD issuing a red alert for seven districts. Relief and rescue operations continued in flood-affected areas, while coastal districts stayed vigilant amid warnings of high waves, sea incursion and possible erosion.
Heavy rain continued to batter Kerala on Friday, prompting the India Meteorological Department (IMD) to issue a red alert for seven districts during the morning hours. Several districts announced a holiday for educational institutions as authorities monitored the situation amid persistent showers.
According to the IMD’s 7 am nowcast bulletin, a red alert was issued for Alappuzha, Kottayam, Ernakulam, Thrissur, Palakkad, Kannur and Kasaragod districts, with isolated areas expected to receive intense rainfall exceeding 15 mm per hour, accompanied by gusty winds reaching up to 50 kmph over the next three hours.
An orange alert was issued for Pathanamthitta, Idukki, Malappuram, Kozhikode and Wayanad districts, where moderate rainfall of 5 mm to 15 mm per hour and wind speeds of up to 50 kmph were forecast at isolated places.
Meanwhile, Thiruvananthapuram, Kollam and Lakshadweep remained under a yellow alert, with light to moderate rainfall below 15 mm per hour and gusty winds of up to 40 kmph expected.
Amid the heavy downpour, district administrations in Ernakulam and Thrissur declared a holiday for educational institutions on Friday. Earlier, similar closures had been announced in Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam, Wayanad, Kannur and Kasaragod districts.

Residents have also been cautioned about the risk of coastal erosion.

Orange Alert issued across Uttar Pradesh; expected rainfall to curb monsoon deficit
Recent data from the IMD highlights significant downpours recorded across various districts in the last 24 hours.
The India meteorological department (IMD) has issued an Orange Alert across Uttar Pradesh, forecasting sustained monsoon activity for the next four to five days. This expected spell of rain offers a vital reprieve for the state, which has faced a cumulative rainfall deficit of 21% since the season began on June 1.
The surge in monsoon activity is driven by a reorganisation of the monsoon trough, which is currently passing near Firozpur, Rohtak, Kanpur, Daltonganj and Digha. According to Mohammad Danish, a senior meteorological officer at the Lucknow observatory, this development coupled with active cyclonic circulations affecting both the lower and upper troposphere is fostering stronger monsoon currents across the Gangetic plains. This shift is expected to alleviate the moisture stress currently impacting 31 districts classified as rain-deficient.
Regarding the state capital, Danish noted that skies over Lucknow will remain generally cloudy, though overall monsoon activity may see a slight reduction in the immediate term.
Recent data from the IMD highlights significant downpours recorded across various districts in the last 24 hours. For the season, Meerut has received the highest rainfall at 624.8 mm, followed by Muzaffarnagar (621 mm) and Gorakhpur (545.3 mm). Conversely, Gautam Buddha Nagar, Ghaziabad, and Kaushambi have recorded the season’s lowest rainfall, at 77.5 mm, 96.3 mm, and 94.4 mm, respectively.
The distribution of the rainfall deficit remains uneven across the state. Bhadohi and Deoria currently record the highest deficits at 70% each, followed by Gautam Buddha Nagar and Kaushambi at 68% each. Regions with the lowest deficits include Chitrakoot (+1%), Bijnor (+1%), Badaun (+4%), and Auraiya (+7%).
The active weather phase is forecast to continue until August 10, bringing widespread rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms. Emphasising the importance of this period, Danish stated, “While the Orange Alert advises local authorities and residents to remain prepared for heavy to very heavy conditions particularly in the next 24 hours this period of sustained activity is crucial. It provides essential replenishment for the state’s reservoirs and agricultural landscape, potentially setting a positive course for the agricultural cycle in regions that have struggled with dryness throughout the monsoon months.”
